question: A 30-year-old woman with moderate persistent asthma (GINA Step 3) has been well-controlled on low-dose ICS-LABA for four months. She is now eight weeks pregnant. What is the most appropriate management?

answers.text: Discontinue the LABA immediately — all LABAs are contraindicated in pregnancy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: LABAs are not categorically contraindicated in pregnancy. Discontinuing effective controller therapy risks exacerbations, which are associated with preterm birth, low birthweight, pre-eclampsia, and foetal hypoxia — all more dangerous than continued inhaled therapy at standard doses.

answers.text: Switch to oral theophylline — it is safer than inhaled agents in pregnancy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic index and requires close therapeutic drug monitoring, which becomes more complex in pregnancy due to altered pharmacokinetics. It is not preferred over ICS-LABA, which delivers drug directly to the airways with minimal systemic absorption.

answers.text: Continue low-dose ICS-LABA — uncontrolled asthma carries greater risk to the foetus than inhaled therapy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Uncontrolled asthma in pregnancy is associated with significant maternal and foetal morbidity (preterm birth, low birthweight, pre-eclampsia, foetal hypoxia). Budesonide has the most reassuring pregnancy safety data among ICS agents. GINA guidelines recommend continuing effective controller therapy during pregnancy.

answers.text: Stop all controllers and use SABA rescue only — minimising drug exposure is safest

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Stepping down to SABA-only in a patient requiring GINA Step 3 therapy risks loss of asthma control. Acute exacerbations during pregnancy cause more harm to the foetus than maintenance inhaled therapy. The principle: controlled asthma on maintenance therapy is safer than uncontrolled asthma on rescue-only treatment.

overallFeedback.feedback: Revisit the clinical decision-making section on special populations. The evidence is clear: uncontrolled asthma poses greater foetal risk than inhaled therapy. Continue effective controllers (especially budesonide-based ICS-LABA) and monitor closely.

Well applied. The key principle: uncontrolled asthma in pregnancy is more dangerous to the foetus than inhaled corticosteroids and LABAs at standard doses. Budesonide has the strongest safety data among ICS agents in pregnancy.
